newsitem.title: THAILAND: ASEAN boosts banking cooperation, cool on currency pact.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN boosts banking cooperation, cool on currency pact.

text.p: Seven Southeast Asian finance ministers ended their first meeting at the weekend with pledges of increased cooperation in banking, customs and insurance.
But they left untouched the issue of possible joint defence of their currencies should they come under heavy attack by speculators.

Finance heads of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) announced on Saturday after a one-day meeting that they would further liberalise banking regulations and give priority to strengthening regional commercial banks facing greater competition because of global financial liberalisation.

They said the statement did not contradict their support for further negotiations among members of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) on liberalisation of financial services scheduled to resume next month.

"We want to have a meaningful cooperative regime using this dialogue to strengthen economies that are non-protectionist and liberalised but to ensure that...regions gain in the process," said Anwar Ibrahim, Malaysia's Finance Minister and Deputy Prime Minister.

The ministers from Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Brunei, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam said their increased cooperation would be key to meeting a target of creating a single market under the ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA) by 2003.
The issue attracting the most media attention was if the group would take steps to deal with future balance of payments problems faced by its members.

The meeting took place after weeks of market attacks on the Thai baht by currency traders and fund managers speculating that the strong U.S. dollar might give Thailand an excuse to devalue its currency to help boost exports.

Speculators were also concerned about the high foreign debt of the Thai private sector and problems faced by some financial institutions from non-performing loans extended to the ailing property sector, as well as the Thai stock market's prolonged slump.
Thailand has repeatedly ruled out any devaluation plan for the baht and has said its $39.2 billion foreign reserves would be sufficient for defending the currency.
A broadly worded communique issued by the ministers did not clarify the fate of a dormant $200 million currency stabilising scheme called the ASEAN Swap Arrangement (ASA).
It said senior officials would review the future role of the inactive mechanism, taking into account dramatic changes in foreign exchange markets since it was first created in 1977.
Three ASEAN members -- Thailand, Malaysia and Singapore -- could tap alternative emergency funds from the $48 billion New Arrangements to Borrow (NAB) of the International Monetary Fund.
They are among 25 potential participants in the NAB, an emergency credit line approved by the IMF executive board in late January.

Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said Thailand had access to a $3.5 billion emergency credit line through bilateral foreign exchange repurchase agreements but he stressed he did not foresee a need to tap it.
His Philippine counterpart Roberto de Ocampo agreed.

"I don't see the need to establish one beyond what we already have through the IMF, and unless they see some compelling reasons to do it, I probably think the IMF for now is an adequate mechanism for this sort of short-term balance of payments management problems."
Singapore officials were also cool to the subject.

De Ocampo backed ASEAN banking reforms saying the Philippines, like its neighbours, had already moved in that direction. But he added the agreement would not dictate the pace for each ASEAN member to take in liberalising banks and financial institutions.

Thai officials said agreements on harmonisation of tariffs and customs clearance procedure, stepped-up anti-smuggling efforts and insurance promotion were the most visible benefits from the meeting that would mean faster goods clearance through ASEAN ports.
